title: Aerosols around the world on 19 August 2025
image_description: A flat world map from NASA's GEOS computer model for 19 August 2025 at 20:00 UTC, showing tiny particles floating in the air. Green is sulfate, mostly from burning fuel and volcanoes, and it streams across the Northern Hemisphere and along coasts. Purple-pink is dust: a huge plume blows west from the Sahara across the Atlantic toward the Caribbean. Grey-blue swirls over the oceans are sea salt whipped up by winds, including a spiral around Hurricane Erin off the US east coast. Orange-red is black carbon smoke, from fires in central and southern Africa and wildfires in Spain. Land is dark grey with city lights. NASA's page names volcanic plumes from Kilauea and Etna among the sulfate.
audio_description:
The sweep lasts 8 seconds and moves from the left edge of the picture to the right edge. The sound moves from your left ear to your right ear with it. On this world map, the left edge is 180 degrees west, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and the right edge is back at the same place, 180 degrees east.
Each kind has its own instrument: Sulfate is the marimba, Dust is the strings, Black carbon (smoke) is the bell, Sea salt is the flute. Higher notes mean the colour sits higher up in the picture (further north). Louder means more of it. Only the two biggest kinds in each slice play, so the sound stays clear.
Sulfate (marimba) is heard most from 0.0 to 0.9 seconds (177 degrees west to 143 degrees west); from 1.5 to 3.1 seconds (110 degrees west to 42 degrees west); from 4.5 to 7.9 seconds (25 degrees east to 172 degrees east).
Dust (strings) is heard most from 2.8 to 4.4 seconds (53 degrees west to 14 degrees east); from 4.8 to 5.1 seconds (37 degrees east to 48 degrees east).
Black carbon (smoke) (bell) is heard most from 4.0 to 4.6 seconds (3 degrees east to 25 degrees east).
Sea salt (flute) is heard most from 7.5 to 7.9 seconds (160 degrees east to 172 degrees east).
credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio. GEOS model, NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office.
